stem: Rajan deposits Rs 2,000 at the end of every year into a savings scheme for 4 years. The scheme pays 10% interest per year compounded annually. Find the future value of this annuity at the end of 4 years. [Given: (1.1)^4 = 1.4641; (1.05)^4 = 1.2155]

per_option_rationale.rationale: Student applies the present-value annuity formula PV = PMT * [1 - (1.1)^(-4)] / 0.1 = 2000 * [1 - 0.6830] / 0.1 = 2000 * 3.170 = Rs 6,340, confusing future value with present value.
Student halves the annual rate to 5% (treating the annual scheme as if it were semi-annual) and computes FV = 2000 * [(1.05)^4 - 1] / 0.05 = 2000 * 0.2155 / 0.05 = 2000 * 4.31 = Rs 8,620.
Student rounds (1.1)^4 to 1.46 (two decimal places) instead of using the given 1.4641, computing FV = 2000 * (1.46 - 1) / 0.1 = 2000 * 4.6 = Rs 9,200.

explanation: For an ordinary annuity (end-of-period payments), FV = PMT * [(1 + r)^n - 1] / r. With PMT = 2000, r = 0.10, n = 4: annuity factor = (1.4641 - 1) / 0.10 = 0.4641 / 0.10 = 4.641. FV = 2000 * 4.641 = Rs 9,282. Using the PV formula instead gives 3.170 * 2000 = Rs 6,340, a common trap at L3.

explanation_sections.punchline: Deposits accumulating to a later date means future value, not present value. Use FV = PMT x [(1+r)^n - 1] / r. The factor is (1.4641 - 1) / 0.10 = 4.641, so FV = 2000 x 4.641 = Rs 9,282.
explanation_sections.approach: Before any arithmetic, settle three questions that pick the formula: are we moving money forward (future value) or back (present value), are payments at the end of each period (ordinary) or the start (due), and does the rate match the payment period. Here it is end-of-year deposits growing to year 4, so FV ordinary annuity. Map the givens: PMT = 2000, r = 0.10, n = 4, and use the supplied (1.1)^4 = 1.4641 rather than recomputing it.
explanation_sections.lesson: Future value uses [(1+r)^n - 1] / r; present value uses [1 - (1+r)^(-n)] / r. Choosing the wrong one is the difference between Rs 9,282 and Rs 6,340. Pick the formula from the direction of time before you touch the numbers.
explanation_sections.timing: About 110 seconds. Spend the first 20 deciding FV versus PV: that one choice kills the Rs 6,340 trap instantly. Use the given power value rather than recomputing it to dodge the rounding trap at Rs 9,200, and keep the stated 10 percent rate to avoid the Rs 8,620 rate-halving trap.
